title: Glenwood Springs Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Glenwood Springs wells have a 128-foot median depth; typical finished-well costs run $12,400-$21,600.
h1: Glenwood Springs Well and Drilling Guide
intro_html:
These records cover permitted wells within five miles of Glenwood Springs in Garfield County. They show a broad range of conditions, with most permits identifying an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer rather than a named basin aquifer.

Use the figures as a starting point for a property review, not as a guarantee for one lot. Only some wells report construction, total depth, yield, or static water level. Neighboring wells, access for a rig, the proposed use, and the site’s geology still control the final result.

sections.heading: Glenwood Springs well depth follows the local ground
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Glenwood Springs is 128 feet. The middle half runs from 60 to 215 feet, so a driller bidding a typical site may be working in that range, while a deeper contingency remains sensible. The recorded range extends to 910 feet, and 3% of wells are deeper than 600 feet.

Depth is not evenly distributed: 39% are under 100 feet, 43% fall between 100 and 300 feet, and 15% are between 300 and 600 feet. The permits mostly name unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer conditions, with 781 wells in that category and 11 in alluvial material. Fractured rock can change quickly from one parcel to the next.

sections.heading: Reported well yields are generally useful, but verify the lot
sections.html:
Among the wells that report a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 10.1 to 15.0 gallons per minute. The records show 64% producing more than 15 gallons per minute, 32% producing between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 4% between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute.

That is encouraging for ordinary household use, but only 142 wells report a yield. A pump test and neighboring well review matter more than the area median for a specific purchase. Colorado exempt household-use wells also have a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit, so a high drilling yield is not the same as unlimited legal use.

sections.heading: Water levels near Glenwood Springs may be getting deeper
sections.html:
The reported median static water level is 59 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 17 to 110 feet. That gives a rough planning range for pump setting and trench work, but static level can vary with season, pumping, recharge, and the measurement method.

Measurements from the 2010s show a median depth to water of 17 feet, compared with 35 feet in the 2020s. The change suggests water levels may be deeper in the newer measurements, but it is not proof of a basin-wide decline. Only 61 wells report a static water level, and the wells and conditions measured may not be comparable. Ask for a current measurement on the property or nearby wells before sizing equipment.

sections.heading: Permit history shows long local drilling experience
sections.html:
Glenwood Springs has a long permit record, with permits issued from the 1950s through the newest recorded year, 2025. The busiest period in the records was the 1990s, with 238 permits, followed by 135 in the 2000s, 96 in the 1980s, and 74 in the 2020s.

The most common driller listed is Shelton Drilling Corporation, associated with Shelton, Wayne, on 283 records. Authorized (Pe, Pg) appears on 98, and Collins Drilling Co, associated with Collins, F. E. “Bodie,” appears on 50. These names help locate comparable permits around No Name and other nearby areas, but an old permit does not confirm present well condition.

sections.heading: What a Glenwood Springs well may cost to drill
sections.html:
The local cost model assumes mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. A typical drilling rate is $50-$75 per foot. At the 128-foot median depth, the drilled hole models to about $6,400-$9,600.

A finished well is more than the hole. Including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, the modeled total is about $12,400-$21,600 at the median depth. A bid can move outside that range when the hole is deeper, access is difficult, casing or grout requirements change, or the site needs more trenching and electrical work. Ask the driller what depth assumption is included, what happens if the hole is dry or low-yield, and which completion items are excluded.

sections.heading: Check water quality, dry-hole risk, and the building site
sections.html:
Mapped environmental information within about ten miles includes 18 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 35 historic mine features. There are 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in that mapped set. Those figures do not certify a particular well as safe. Test existing or new well water for contaminants relevant to the property’s location and history, and review nearby mine and industrial land uses.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible even where area statistics look strong, especially in fractured bedrock. Confirm well location, casing, grout, pump capacity, and water-quality results. Septic setbacks, drainfield soil, driveway access, and the house footprint must work together. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required for new uses, so check the permit conditions with Colorado DWR before designing the project.

sections.heading: A practical purchase plan for Glenwood Springs land
sections.html:
Start with the Colorado DWR permit map and compare wells close to the parcel, especially around No Name, Chacra, Cattle Creek, and New Castle. Look for reported depth, yield, static level, aquifer description, construction details, and the permitted use. The local records are mostly domestic or household permits at 51%; monitoring wells make up 35%, while irrigation is 4% and stock is 2%. A monitoring well is not a household-water comparison.

Before closing, make the purchase contingent on a qualified well inspection, water test, and septic evaluation. If building, obtain a written drilling estimate that states access, depth assumptions, completion components, and low-yield terms. Confirm the permit allows the intended use and that an augmentation plan is not needed. The median is useful for budgeting, but the closest comparable wells are the better guide for this lot.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Glenwood Springs?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Glenwood Springs is 128 feet. The middle half is 60 to 215 feet, but the records reach 910 feet. About 39% are under 100 feet and 43% are between 100 and 300 feet. Fractured-bedrock conditions mean nearby wells can still differ substantially.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Glenwood Springs?
faq.a: The local model uses $50-$75 per foot. At the 128-foot median depth, drilling the hole models to $6,400-$9,600. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $12,400-$21,600. Get a written bid that explains depth assumptions, access charges, and what happens if yield is poor.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Glenwood Springs?
faq.a: Reported well yields have a 15.0-gallon-per-minute median, with the middle half from 10.1 to 15.0 gallons per minute. The records show 64% above 15 gallons per minute and 4% between 1 and 5. Only 142 wells report yield, so request a pump test or nearby comparable records for the property.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Glenwood Springs?
faq.a: The area has 18 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 35 historic mine features within about ten miles. There are 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in that mapped set. These facts do not establish safety for an individual well. Test the property’s water and review nearby mine, industrial, and other possible contamination sources.

faq.q: Are water levels falling near Glenwood Springs?
faq.a: Reported median depth to water was 17 feet in measurements from the 2010s and 35 feet in the 2020s. That may indicate deeper recent water levels, but only 61 wells report static water level, and measurements may not be comparable. The overall median is 59 feet below surface, with a middle half from 17 to 110 feet.
